Let’s dive into Chapter 5: Empowering Young People to Take Antiracist Action.
You know, it can feel overwhelming—like the problems of racism and inequality are just too big for any one person to take on. But if you look back through history, real change almost always starts with people who dare to ask tough questions and refuse to settle for the world as it is. And more often than not, it’s young people who stand up first and push for something better.
Picture this: there’s a student who notices the books in their school library don’t really reflect the diversity of the students walking those halls. Instead of just shrugging it off, they decide to talk to a teacher, rally some classmates, and kick off a campaign for more inclusive books. Sure, at first, they face some pushback. Some folks say, “Isn’t that too hard to change?” or “Does it really matter?” But that student doesn’t give up—and little by little, the library begins to look a lot more like the students it serves.
Taking antiracist action doesn’t always mean leading a march or giving a big speech. Sometimes, it’s about listening—really listening—to others, learning about the past, and being open to changing your own perspective. It’s about spotting those moments when something just isn’t fair, and choosing to do something about it. That could be standing up for a classmate, speaking out in a discussion, or joining a group that’s working for change.
Here’s something to pay attention to: moving beyond just being “not racist.” It’s not enough to simply avoid saying or doing hurtful things. Real progress comes when you’re willing to challenge unfairness, even if it feels uncomfortable. That might mean having tough conversations with family or friends, or questioning rules and traditions that don’t seem right.
And let’s be real—nobody gets it right all the time. We all make mistakes, and sometimes old habits creep back in. What matters is the willingness to learn, to listen, and to keep showing up. Antiracism isn’t something you check off a list—it’s a journey that keeps evolving.
Throughout history, it’s been young people leading the way—think about the sit-ins during the civil rights movement, or the student-led campaigns we see today. Their courage and energy spark others to join in. The work is tough, and there’ll always be people saying, “Is it really worth it?” But every step forward—even the small ones—add up and make a difference.
The story of racism in America is long and complicated, but here’s the thing—it’s not over yet. Every new generation gets a chance to write a different ending, one where fairness and respect aren’t the exception, but the rule. The first step? Just believing that change is possible, and being willing to take action, no matter how small.
